_meta.purpose: Plain-language glossary for terms used in the tax breakdown app. Intended for inline tooltips/definitions (e.g. a (?) icon next to the term), not a standalone glossary page nobody reads.

terms.short_definition: The dollar figure the county uses to calculate your tax bill -- usually lower than what your home would actually sell for.
terms.longer_note: Oregon law limits how fast assessed value can grow each year, so in many cases it's well below market value, especially for homes that have been owned a long time.

terms.short_definition: The county's estimate of what your property would sell for today.
terms.longer_note: This is different from assessed value (see above) and is not what your tax bill is based on.

terms.short_definition: How much you pay per $1,000 of assessed value.
terms.longer_note: Example: a rate of $2.50 means you pay $2.50 for every $1,000 of your property's assessed value. A $300,000 assessed home at that rate pays $750/year for that one district.

terms.short_definition: A tax a district is authorized to collect.
terms.longer_note: Districts don't set their own rate freely -- their levy is approved either permanently (voted in once, applies every year) or as a local option (voted in for a limited number of years).

terms.short_definition: A tax rate that was voted in once and continues every year without needing renewal.
terms.longer_note: Most of the county, school, and fire district base rates are permanent rates.

terms.short_definition: An additional tax rate voters approved for a limited number of years, on top of the permanent rate.
terms.longer_note: These expire and have to be renewed by voters, unlike permanent rates.

terms.short_definition: A tax specifically for paying back money borrowed for a big one-time project, like a new school or hospital building.
terms.longer_note: Bonds are temporary -- they end once the borrowed money is paid off, usually after 15-20 years. They're listed separately from a district's regular operating rate.

terms.short_definition: A program where a city sets aside a slice of tax growth in a specific district to fund improvement projects there (like downtown revitalization).
terms.longer_note: It doesn't directly add to your tax rate the way other districts do -- instead it redirects some of the growth in property value within the renewal area toward local improvement projects, which can mean other districts collect slightly less from that specific area.

terms.short_definition: A small zone where every property is taxed by the exact same combination of districts.
terms.longer_note: Curry County has about 45 of these. Two neighbors can be in different code areas -- and pay different total rates -- if one is covered by a different fire or water district.

terms.short_definition: Any local government or agency allowed to collect property tax, like a school district, fire district, or library district.
terms.longer_note: Curry County has around 48 separate taxing districts. Most properties fall within somewhere between 6 and 12 of them at once.

terms.short_definition: A constitutional cap that can reduce your tax bill if the combined rate for schools or general government gets too high.
terms.longer_note: This is a technical Oregon-specific safeguard; most residents won't need this explained beyond 'there's a legal ceiling on how high your combined rate can go.'
